content.thinking:
I'm checking the root cause claim: the rewritten average_spend_per_item is the branch used when neither rollout flag is set, and that's supported by the render_spend_summary logic. It recomputes the total from the purchase list rather than using a carried total, and the loops copy and re-sum the prefix on each pass, so the work grows with the square of the input. Only the last pass's sum ends up being used.

I'm checking the rest of the root cause claims, and the symptom holds up since the log lines all come from account pages and the p95 latency series backs it. The slow requests rose sharply from the onset while error rates stayed within normal variation. The deploy of 5e07d73 landed during the onset minute on every replica, and I'm now looking at whether the earlier 70dbcfd deploy could explain it, using the metrics from that deploy up to the onset.

I'm checking the remaining claims against the record: the rollback to the earlier revision is supported, and the causal chain holds up on the figures I've already read. The contributing factors don't add anything new. Nothing in the record shows a test checking cost, only one asserting the result on a two-purchase account, and there's no sign of a staged rollout, since the revision landed on every replica at once.

I'm checking the last of the incident record: no one was paged while the incident ran, and the record itself calls that a finding of its own. That holds up, so I'll keep it.

supported.quote: The rewritten average_spend_per_item, the lifetime-average calculation the account page uses whenever neither rollout flag is set, works out the total from the purchase list instead of reading the total the account already carries.
It does this by looping over the purchases and, on every pass, copying and re-summing the whole list up to that point.
The work per request therefore grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count, even though only the last pass's sum is used.

A code change to how the shop works out a shopper's average spend made it add up the shopper's purchases again and again instead of once, so the work grew steeply with the number of things a shopper had bought.
Account pages could slow down again if revision 5e07d73, or any later revision that still has its spend calculation, is deployed to io-shop.
Account pages on the shop loaded slowly
Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly. The response time of io-shop's slowest requests rose far above its usual level from the onset, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation.
rows: Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation

supported.quote: The slow requests started when io-shop began serving revision 5e07d73. It was deployed during the onset minute, and every replica was running it as of the deployment-status read.

The earlier deploy of revision 70dbcfd. The metrics read back cover the hours from that deploy to the onset and show the service at its normal latency until the onset minute. The service was also measured back to normal once that revision was running again.

That revision rewrote average_spend_per_item, which render_spend_summary uses for the account page whenever neither rollout flag is set. It now works out the lifetime total from the shopper's purchase list instead of dividing the total the account already carries.
The new loop re-sums the whole purchase list up to each position on every pass, so each account-page request does work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count.

No test was seen that checks how the cost of the account-page spend calculation grows with a long purchase history. The test the change added checks only the result, on an account with a short purchase list.

No staged rollout was seen. The revision was running on every io-shop replica as of the deployment-status read, and no step was seen that served it to a slice of traffic and checked latency before the rest.
Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person on call was brought in while the incident ran.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one
